catalog_quote: [3.2.2 Metrical structure] Weak positions in metrical structure are characterized by raising and/or reduction of short vowels. Metrical structure is not a major factor in BenT in (uncompounded) noun, adjective, or numeral stems. The initial syllable is arguably a strong position, and there are many bisyllabic stems with an initial heavy syllable, e.g. bɔ̀:tɔ́ ‘sack’, jɛ́mbɛ́ ‘bag’. However, nouns like sègérè ‘filtering basket’ show no phonological signs of strong and weak positions; in particular, the second syllable of a trisyllabic stem is stable. ... In verbs, there are some suggestions of metrical structure insofar as some types of nonmonosyllabic verb stems show alternations between final a and a somewhat unstable high vowel {i u}. ... So metrical structure plays a relatively small role in BenT phonology. [2.1 Prosody] The syllabic tones in BenT, whether lexical or grammatical, are H, L, <HL>, <LH>, and bell-shaped <LHL>. ... Stems (except for some expressive adverbials) must have at least one H-tone. The normal lexical melodies are /H/, /HL/, /LH/, /LHL/, and /HLH/ ... [3.7 Tones] Tones at the level of syllables are H[igh], L[ow], <LH> (rising), <HL> (falling), and bell-shaped <LHL>.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ben Tey is described purely as a tone language (syllable tones H, L, rising, falling, bell-shaped; lexical stem melodies; grammatical tone overlays). Heath never posits word stress or accent. The only prominence-related statement is metrical: the word-initial syllable is 'arguably' a strong position (non-initial short high vowels in verbs may raise/reduce/apocopate), but metrical structure is explicitly said to play a relatively small role; no stress placement rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: Trisyllabic nouns like sègérè show no strong/weak asymmetry; medial syllable of trisyllabic stems is stable; final short high vowels {i u} of CvCi stems may apocopate (Sec. 3.5.3.2); verbs with final a ~ high-vowel alternation show weak-position behaviour of the final vowel.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns stem/word-internal metrical structure (uncompounded noun, adjective, numeral, verb stems); prosody chapter otherwise about lexical/grammatical tone and clause-final intonation (Sec. 3.8). 'Stress' appears in the grammar only in glosses about English.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Ben Tey (BenT) of Beni village and neighbouring hamlets, Mali = Glottolog bent1238 / ISO dbt exactly; Heath groups it with Bankan Tey and Nanga.

tone_statements.citation: Heath, Jeffrey. 2015. Dogon lexical tones of stems. Unpublished cross-Dogon typology report, Dogon and Bangime Linguistics (dogonlanguages.info).
tone_statements.quote: Like all Dogon languages, it has a phonemic distinction between L and H tone, though it additionally shows surface underspecified syllables (Ø), which receive F0 through interpolation (McPherson 2011). Importantly, almost all Dogon languages have a ban on lexically /L/ words; this means that the most common overlay, {L}, is always audibly distinct from lexical tone. Additional data are drawn from Ben Tey (Heath 2013a), Jamsay … Ben Tey has very complicated rules of tonal allomorphy for the possessive overlay, relying on details of both syntactic structure of the possessor and on its ﬁnal tone.
tone_statements.locator: p. 5, sec. 2 'Dogon languages' + p. 37 fn. 22, sec. 6.1 'Hierarchical reversals'; Ben Tey exx. (35), (37) pp. 37-39
tone_statements.summary: Phonemic H vs L tone (stated for all Dogon languages); Ben Tey lexical noun tones are overwritten by word-level grammatical overlays {HL} (possessor) and {L} (adjective, demonstrative).

tone_statements.citation: Heath, Jeffrey. 2015. Dogon noncompositional constructional tonosyntax. Journal of African Languages and Linguistics 36(2): 233-252.
tone_statements.quote: Syllables may bear high ǀHǀ or low ǀLǀ, likely a feature going back to Niger-Congo (Hyman et al. 2020: 183). • One H stretch = Lexical items in Tommo So, Yorno So & Donno So contain exactly one H tone stretch. • Open class stems (nouns, adjectives, numerals, verbs ) normally contain at least one syllable bearing a high tone ǀHǀ or contain ǀHǀ as part of a rising ǀLHǀ or falling ǀHLǀ contour tone (Heath & McPherson 2013; McPherson 2013; Heath 2016).
tone_statements.locator: handout p. 2, sec. 2 'Phonotactics and Tonotactics of Dogon' (bullets 2-4)
tone_statements.summary: Cross-Dogon handout: Dogon syllables bear high or low tone (rising/falling written as LH/HL); So-language lexical items have one H stretch; compound dependents drop to all-low. No Ben Tey forms.

tone_statements.citation: Heath, Jeffrey. 2014. Dogon tonosyntax of NP. Unpublished cross-Dogon typology report, Dogon and Bangime Linguistics (dogonlanguages.info).
tone_statements.quote: The transcription system used for the Dogon languages is basically IPA … There are two phonemic tones, H and L, marked with acute (v́) and grave (v̀) accents, respectively; unmarked syllables are toneless. … In Ben Tey, the 1sg pronoun is a tonal morpheme L that concatenates with a {HL} overlay … the 1sg floating L links to the first syllable of the possessed noun. The H of the {HL} possessive overlay also links to this syllable, with L tones subsequently. Interestingly, as (8b) shows, this can lead to contour tones on light syllables, a pattern that does not occur lexically in Ben Tey.
tone_statements.summary: Two phonemic tones, H and L, with toneless syllables (stated for the Dogon sample incl. Ben Tey); Ben Tey possessors impose {HL} or {L} tone overlays; the 1sg possessor is a floating L tone.

tone_statements.citation: Heath, Jeffrey & Laura McPherson. 2013. Tonosyntax and reference restriction in Dogon NPs. Language 89(2): 265-296. DOI 10.1353/lan.2013.0020.
tone_statements.quote: The analysis presented here is broadly valid, mutatis mutandis, for most Dogon languages, including Ben Tey, Nanga, Bankan Tey, Toro Tegu, Jamsay, Tommo So, Najamba, Togo Kan (and related varieties), and Yorno So (and the rest of ‘Toro So’).[fn. 3:] Yanda Dom, Tebul Ure, and Tiranige have somewhat similar systems but some important differences. Donno So, Dogulu, and Tomo Kan are currently under study by colleagues. A western Dogon subgroup including Mombo, Ampari, Bunoge, and Penange has a more divergent NP tonosyntax and requires separate treatment; see Prokhorov 2011 on NP tonosyntax in Mombo.
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Bunoge (with Mombo, Ampari, Penange) has NP tonosyntax that diverges from the mainstream Dogon controller/overlay system; no further detail given here.

sources.note: Family-level overview of Dogon NP tone overlays: H and L tones, lexical stem melodies {H} {HL} {LH} {LHL}, floating tonal morphemes, {L}/{HL} overlays; Ben Tey is not named or described.

tone.quote: Tonal processes are critical in the grammatical systems of Dogon languages. There are several types of tonal configuration: o lexical tone melodies associated with specific lexical items … o tonal morphemes (affixes and clitics), each consisting of a “floating” tone (H or L) that is realized on a neighboring morpheme; o word- or stem-level tone overlays … Most Dogon languages have a constraint on noun, verb, adjective, and numeral stems against all-low lexical tone melodies. This means that lexical melodies may be {H}, {HL}, {LH}, {LHL}, and in some languages also {HLH}, but not {L}.
